summary: Describes TMux, a protocol that combines many small transport segments, whatever application they belong to, into fewer packets between a terminal server and a host. The aim is to cut the overhead of lots of tiny packets. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of mailing many tiny letters one by one, you put them in one envelope. TMux does that for small chunks of data.

questions: how to combine small packets between server and host
subtitle: Bundling many small packets into one to reduce network overhead from interactive sessions.

tldr.problem: Terminal servers and interactive applications like Telnet generate many tiny packets; the overhead of processing them strains networks and host CPUs more than the actual data volume.
tldr.mechanism: TMux multiplexes multiple transport segments (TCP or UDP packets) into a single IP datagram, with a small header preceding each segment to identify its protocol and length.
tldr.outcome: The protocol was never widely deployed; modern network speeds and TCP improvements made it less necessary. It is now Historic.

today: RFC 1692 is Historic. While the protocol was designed to optimize terminal server traffic, it was never widely deployed. Modern high-speed networks, TCP improvements, and the decline of terminal servers made the overhead reduction less compelling. The protocol remains a notable example of layer optimization that did not find broad adoption.

sections.title: The Small-Packet Problem
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, terminal servers connected many users to a few hosts. When many users typed on their Telnet or Rlogin sessions at once, each keystroke—just one character—would generate a tiny packet. A host must do nearly as much work to process a 1-byte packet as a 1500-byte packet: the cost is in interrupt handling and header processing, not in the data itself. With many interactive sessions on a terminal server, the per-packet overhead became the network and host performance bottleneck, not the volume of data.

TMux (Transport Multiplexing Protocol) addresses this by combining many small transport segments destined for the same host into a single IP datagram, reducing the number of packets and the per-packet overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer gets tired because many people are sending tiny messages. If you put all the tiny messages in one big package, your computer gets less tired. TMux does that.

sections.title: TMux Header and Packet Structure
sections.content:
TMux operates at the IP layer, using protocol number 18. When a host wants to multiplex transport segments, it strips the IP header from each segment and prepends a TMux mini-header (4 octets), then concatenates all the segments into one IP datagram. The mini-header contains the protocol ID (what protocol this segment is—TCP, UDP, etc.), the total length of this segment including the mini-header, and a checksum covering only the mini-header.

Segments may be padded to maintain 32-bit alignment, but the length field reports the actual segment length, not the padded length. A TMux message thus appears as: IP header | mini-header | segment | mini-header | segment | ... The receiving host demultiplexes the segments and hands them to the transport layer, which is unaware of the special encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tiny message gets a label saying what kind of message it is, how big it is, and a check mark. Then many labeled messages go in one big envelope.

sections.title: Negotiation and Maintaining Capability
sections.content:
Since not all hosts support TMux, the protocol includes a negotiation mechanism: a host sends a TMux ENQ (enquiry) message—an IP datagram with protocol 18 and no payload—to ask if a peer supports TMux. If the peer supports TMux, it sends data in TMux format; if not, the sender falls back to standard IP datagrams. The sender maintains a time-to-live (TTL) for each peer's TMux capability; if no TMux data is received for a timeout period (e.g., one minute), the capability expires and the sender re-ENQs.

This design allows transparent switching between TMux and standard IP without affecting transport protocols. However, if a peer reboots and stops supporting TMux, it may take a reboot or timeout for others to detect the change.
sections.plainLanguage: Before bundling messages, you ask the other person: "Do you accept bundled messages?" If they say yes (by sending bundled messages back), you know it is safe. If they do not answer, you stop bundling after a while.

sections.title: Multiplexing Timing and Configuration
sections.content:
When a segment is ready to send, TMux adds it to a Multiplexed Message under construction for that destination host. A timer is started when the first segment arrives; when the timer expires, the message is sent. If the buffer fills before the timer expires, the message is sent immediately. The delay should be user-configurable, typically 20 to 30 milliseconds—long enough to collect multiple segments but short enough to avoid user-visible delays in interactive sessions. Recommended practice is to not multiplex segments larger than 700 octets (to avoid introducing latency on large transfers) and to restrict multiplexing to interactive protocols like Telnet and Rlogin based on port numbers.

Configurations may also limit the number of segments per message or set other thresholds.
sections.plainLanguage: When the first tiny message arrives, start a timer. Wait a little while to see if more messages come. When the timer rings or the envelope fills up, mail it. Big messages do not wait in line.

sections.title: Security and Practical Considerations
sections.content:
TMux does not add security mechanisms; security is the responsibility of upper-layer protocols. One concern: if a firewall filters packets based on TCP port numbers, TMux-multiplexed segments are not subject to that filtering because the port numbers are inside the payload. However, large segments from the same connection are still sent as regular IP datagrams and are subject to filtering, creating an inconsistency. Routers that do not support TMux should drop TMux packets to ensure consistent filtering behavior.

Practical notes include: do not multiplex segments with IP options, use only unicast addresses, and avoid the loopback address. If a TMux implementation is sending many single-segment messages (no actual multiplexing benefit), TMux should be disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: TMux does not keep secrets—other protocols do that. One tricky thing: if someone is checking what kind of message goes through, they might miss bundled messages.
